notes.1a: (i) Most candidates gained at least partial credit for giving the correct orders with respect to reactants but some did not refer to data in table, as required by the question.
notes.1aii: Many candidates carried out the calculation correctly, although many ignored the need for two significant figures, as required by the question.
notes.1iii: Most candidates were able to give a correct equation.
notes.1iv: Many candidates carried out the calculation correctly giving the correct units of k. A common error was k being calculated using incorrect experimental data.
notes.1b: Most candidates gained at least partial credit here, though the shape and clarity of many curves needed to be improved. Many candidates needed to be more precise with their explanations.
notes.1c: Many candidates did not realise that the orders suggested that one molecule of F2 and one molecule of NO were involved in the rate determining slow step. �PAGE�33
notes.2a: This question was not well answered, with many candidates not applying the rules of orbital occupancy for the nickel atom. For the formation of the ion, some candidates incorrectly removed d electrons.
notes.2b: (i) Many candidates gave the correct answer here.
notes.2bii: There were some good answers, although many candidates did not recall that lower energy d orbitals have each of the lobes pointing between two of the axes or that higher energy d orbitals have their lobes pointing along the axes.
notes.2c: Most candidates gained credit here. Some candidates did not describe the promotion of an electron from a lower to a higher level by the absorption of visible light, or the colour transmitted (not emitted) being the complement of the colour absorbed.
notes.2d: Many candidates gained partial credit here using their knowledge of Cu chemistry to answer this question. A was Ni(OH)2 and both 4-coordinated and six-coordinated complexes of B were credited. A common error was unbalanced equations.
notes.3a: (i) Many candidates correctly identified the isotopic composition of the three fragments.
notes.3aii: This was generally well answered. The most common error was the relative ratio of 9:3:1.
notes.3b: (i) Almost all candidates gave the correct answer here.
notes.3bii: Many candidates answered correctly here. The octahedral sketch was generally better drawn than the tetrahedral one. Some candidates incorrectly displayed a square planar sketch for [PCl 4] + .
notes.3c: (i) A pleasing number of candidates correctly identified one of the variations. Common errors were phosphorus with four bonds or oxygen with three bonds.
notes.3cii: Almost all gave the correct answer here.
notes.3d: (i) Many candidates gave a correct expression for Ksp here. Common errors were incorrect charges on the ions and the powers of concentration.
notes.3dii: Although ‘error carried forward’ from (i) was used, it was unusual for candidates to be awarded more than partial credit. A common error was incorrect calculation of the concentrations of the two ions. Many candidates gained credit for their units.
notes.3e: (i) Most candidates gave the correct definition of the lattice energy. Weaker answers involved the description of a mole of ionic compound being formed from 1 mole of its gaseous ions.
notes.3eii: Many candidates managed to suggest a valid reason here.
notes.4a: (i) This was generally well answered, although there were many incorrect or unbalanced equations.
notes.4aii: Most candidates gained at least partial credit here. The direction and source of curly arrows proved problematic as did the drawing of the intermediate.
notes.4b: (i)(ii) The explanation required here should have been learnt. Whilst the majority of candidates knew that ethanoic acid was less acidic than chloroethanoic acid, and that ethanol was less acidic than phenol, many did not relate these acidities to valid explanations. �PAGE�34
notes.4c: Many candidates seemed unable to draw upon knowledge from a range of areas of the organic chemistry syllabus here. The type of reaction with Na and the reaction with hot excess NaOH(aq) proved difficult.
notes.5a: Candidates should be aware of the relative rate of hydrolysis of these organohalogen compounds. Although some candidates gave the correct order of hydrolysis, the explanation in terms of C-Cl bond strength was not always given.
notes.5b: Most candidates identified the correct functional groups here but should note that vague terms such as carbonyl or carboxylic are not detailed enough for credit to be awarded.
notes.5c: (i) Again, candidates need to be sure of the methods used for drawing curly arrows in such a reaction mechanism.
notes.5cii: Many candidates were able to give the correct mechanism.
notes.5iii: Most candidates correctly identified HBr. However CH3Br was a common incorrect answer.
notes.5d: Most candidates gained at least partial credit here. W and Y were more commonly correct than X. Candidates need to take care when drawing structures to avoid mistakes. X was often incorrectly drawn as an ester.
notes.5e: Candidates should be reminded to read the question. Here they were asked to give two repeat units; this was very often not seen.
notes.6a: This was generally well answered by candidates.
notes.6b: (i) Many candidates did not recognise a solvent was required for the mobile phase or Al 2O3 (or SiO2) for the stationary phase. A common error was confusing this technique with column chromatography or electrophoresis.
notes.6bii: Candidates gave mixed answers here. Partition was a common error.
notes.6c: Most candidates gained some credit here although often did not concentrate on structural aspects of DNA.
notes.6d: Many candidates answered this question well.
notes.7a: Candidates were asked to circle the bonds that could be easily hydrolysed but many circled the functional groups instead.
notes.7b: Many candidates were able to give a correct answer here.
notes.7c: This was answered well by candidates.
notes.7d: Almost all candidates gave the correct answer here.
notes.8a: (i) The calculation of the number of carbon atoms was carried out successfully by most candidates.
notes.8aii: A good number of candidates correctly stated the molecular formula of T, although a common error was C4H9OH. �PAGE�35
notes.8b: (i) Some candidates managed to correctly identify the structure of T. Many incorrectly suggested butan-2-ol.
notes.8bii: (iii) Most candidates gained at least partial credit here. Candidates were required to identify the type of proton responsible for each of the absorptions in T and to do this should have consulted the Data Booklet. From some of the answers given it did not seem likely that candidates had used their Data Booklets.
notes.8iv: Many candidates identified that the OH peak would not be present in D2O. �PAGE�36

equations.
(cid:127) Candidates are reminded of the importance of careful, thorough reading of the question before
attempting to answer.
(cid:127) Candidates should set out calculations with clear explanations of the numbers involved. This is
especially important where Examiners are able to apply credit for error carried forward.
(cid:127) Candidates should be reminded of the need to re-visit and revise AS material while preparing for the A
Level examination.
